questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

questions.problem:
Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

where 

$$
s-6>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+6.
$$

Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s+5),
$$

where 

$$
s+5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-5.
$$

questions.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $5$ units to the right.
